steps.title: The northern Rhône
steps.body: Marsanne is the main white grape of the northern Rhône's Hermitage, Crozes-Hermitage, Saint-Joseph and Saint-Péray, where it also makes sparkling wine. It's often blended with Roussanne, which adds aroma, acidity and finesse. In the south, it appears in Côtes du Rhône blends.

steps.title: Roussanne
steps.body: Roussanne, its partner, has russet skins, from roux, and gives more aromatic, herbal, elegant wines, with better acidity. But it's harder to grow, prone to disease and irregular yields. Marsanne gives body and reliability; Roussanne gives perfume and freshness. Together they make balanced blends.
steps.highlight: Marsanne for body; Roussanne for freshness

steps.prompt: Match each grape to its contribution.
steps.explanation: Rhône whites are built from complementary grapes.

steps.title: Victoria
steps.body: Australia's Victoria has some of the world's oldest Marsanne vines, at Tahbilk, in the Nagambie Lakes, planted in 1927. Tahbilk's Marsanne is unoaked, lean and citrus when young, turning honeyed and toasty after 10 years. It shows how well Marsanne can age.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Marsanne leads the whites of Hermitage and Saint-Joseph
